title: This shit can be so frustrating... but I love it
author: 710cartman
selftext:
I would get hate for this in a lot of subs, but:

I've always wanted to do game design. When I was a little kid, I told my parents I wanted to learn Japanese so I could help make Nintendo games (yeah, I know that's dumb asf in hindsight but I was like, 5 years old).

But life happens and I never learned to really code. When I was younger I got into some script writing and made some shitty HTML pages, but never "real" coding. I also went through a Photoshop phase, but never "real" graphics design. 

And now, I can be a lead game designer. Maybe my game never makes a penny and no one plays it but me while iterating. And for sure, sometimes it's frustrating in many ways.

But damn if it isn't everything I thought it would be. I really do love it.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
It can be frustrating but moreso when you code yourself. I was a game designer in the mid 2000s and even with large teams it can get frustrating when your code won't work right.

It's funny and almost jarring to NOT be looking at lines of code all day. Instead that's replaced with a robot with the temperament of a toddler.

"NO god damn it, why are you adding the NPCs from stage 1 to stage 2??"
"Well you said add NPCs so I just added them all. Also here's an extra lifebar, and I've gone ahead and removed your debug tool."

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: It is weird. I used to code all of my games line by line in vanilla JS. Now, I am never looking at code. Pretty weird. I do miss the satisfaction of seeing things work after so much debugging, but it's impossible to go back in our current landscape.

replies.author: ginger_beer_m
replies.body: I know that feeling. I haven't looked at actual lines of codes and wondering why it didn't work while it actually should, kind of miss this feeling as this is what we used to do all day long. And instead now it's replaced by an autistic magic genie that kind of does what we want but often not getting it right.

comments.author: Timely_Spirit_9053
comments.body: ive been directing a game, i love seeing it come nicely to be more and more playable, i already added a good amount of content and am now trying to polish the rest of the functions before i keep going, its a fun little hobby to do in my free time

comments.author: Timely_Spirit_9053
comments.body: Perhaps, i cant say i understand exactly how non AI devs felt but i understand part of it, but thats the beauty of it, with AI its so extremely easy to both polish and eliminate bugs, you dont even need to do EVERYTHING, but you shouldnt ditch a tool that save you time, AI is a godsend for coders, why wouldnt you want a software that can detect the issue when you point it out, and either fix it for you or advise how to solve it.

comments.author: rvl_16
comments.body:
Same bro, I think we're maybe same age? I grew up with C64 and then NES 8 bit, SNES 16 bit and then N64. 

Always dreamt of making my own game. Also did html, photoshop. Still do the latter. But never had talent or interest in programming. Now Claude does the work for me. Nearly 44 years old here, got 2 young kids, almost 0 spare time

But man, I love my Claude - unity - blender - asesprite setup so far

comments.author: delicious_pubes
comments.body:
I have been working as a professional game designer for over a decade and as a hobby much longer, all I can say is welcome and I’m glad you’re having fun!

The fun part is that AI still can’t do game design so you get to actually learn-by-doing. I think AI is best for designers because you really get a fast feedback loop and can learn lessons faster than ever before. I’ve mostly been making games outside of my comfort zone so I’m learning a lot about design jn genres that I haven’t had the opportunity to work in professionally yet. The downside is that a lot of people doing this for the first time don’t realize that AI can’t design and when people shit on their games it’s because the games are shitty.

replies.author: ginger_beer_m
replies.body: Do you have resources, articles, books, videos etc to learn more about game designing? I know the best way is probably to learn by doing and copying others (just like any other arts) but wouldn't mind some recommendation of things to read between prompting lol.

replies.author: delicious_pubes
replies.body:
For resources the main thing when you start is to learn to think like a designer and get into that headspace. For that I recommend “the art of game design” by Jesse Schell and “the design of everyday things”. Neither is a bible but will help you understand how designers think about problems. There’s also the book “flow” which is less required reading as much as understanding the concept itself is a requirement, you can look to YouTube for a tl;dr on that.

A fun watch is Sakurai’s videos on design that he did a short series of on YouTube. And GMTK is a respected source for game design analysis but not so much for how to arrive at design answers. Also GDC talks are always great especially for particular examples (I just watched the one on amnesia’s design to help me understand how they got their dread affect)

The most important thing is to make stuff, armchair designers are useless and even with all these resources available they are full of bad ideas because only experience can make you a good designer.

When I started I cloned small arcade games like stack or flappy bird and the truth is that those games have a ton of micro decisions that made them great, even though they’re dead simple and it helped me have a deeper appreciation for their designs. AI changes the landscape a lot more since cloning a simple game is a one shot prompt, but if you scope up just a little more you’ll find ways to learn these lessons.

Have fun!
